chapter: Tuba in jazz history and technique
title: Gil Evans: 'sounds just like a bass'
summary: Stewart tried to sound like a bass until Gil Evans's comment led him to recover the tuba's own sound and New Orleans feeling.

blocks.x: But it sure — the sound of the tuba now is indelible with sort of an era of music and it still has its place. Now you’ve been trying to move it —

Because it’s an interesting story. I was, for many years I took great pleasure when people would say, because I’d been working hard to try and do the bass thing and people would say, “Wow Bob, sounds great, it sounds just like a bass.” I’d get all proud and just stick my chest out, you know what I mean? Because that’s what I’d been trying to do, just to find the technique of how to make that role and feel like a bass player playing. And so I put a quartet together, Jon Clarke and I, a French horn player. And taped it, and it was in the early eighties when I did this, it was after I’d been working with Gil Evans. So I took the tape down to Gil Evans and let him hear it. And everyone else had been saying, “Wow, sounds great, Bob, sounds just like a bass.” And Gil said to me, he used exactly the same words except he put emphasis on a different syllable. All right? He said, “Yeah, Bob, sounds great, but it just sounds like a bass.” So I discovered, in all my efforts to try and sound like and reproduce that feeling of a bass I’d lost an instrument. I totally lost the tuba in my efforts. So I actively went about finding the instrument that I lost in order to, like I say, going both ways. So a lot of my compositions are influenced by New Orleans © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
and the feelings of that style of music. So I have, I think one of the tunes on, it’s called “Hambone.” And it has that New Orleans kind of feeling to it.
